stories.headline: Jobs shock sinks Friday tape: S&P 7,718.60, Dow 53,414, Nasdaq 26,507
stories.dek: August payrolls +162k (vs ~56k expected) revived September hike bets. 2-year yield ~4.37%. Markets closed Monday for Labor Day.
stories.caveman: Friday was a down day. The S&P 500 fell 29.11 points to 7,718.60 (−0.4%). The Dow lost 272 to 53,414.25 (−0.5%). The Nasdaq slipped 77 to 26,506.99 (−0.3%). Why? The U.S. said employers added 162,000 jobs in August — almost three times what Wall Street guessed. That made people think the Fed might raise rates again. The 2-year Treasury yield jumped to about 4.37%. U.S. markets are shut Monday for Labor Day.
stories.why_it_matters: Hot jobs can mean higher borrowing costs for homes, cards, and companies. The next big clues are PPI and CPI next week before the Sept. 15–16 Fed meeting.
stories.camps: Hawks say strong hiring gives the Fed room to hike. Soft-landing camp says one hot month is not a full cycle, and chips still rallied.

terms.explain: Index of 500 big U.S. companies. A quick market mood meter.
Official U.S. count of new jobs outside farming.
U.S. central bank that sets key interest rates.
What lenders earn on 2-year U.S. government bonds. Often moves with rate-hike bets.

stories.image_alt: Wall Street after the Friday close

stories.headline: Brent hits $96.28 as U.S.–Iran tanker war squeezes Hormuz oil
stories.dek: Friday close highest since July 24. U.S. diesel set a record ~$5.85/gal. Hormuz flows still far below pre-war levels.
stories.caveman: Oil got more expensive. Brent crude finished Friday at $96.28 a barrel — the highest since late July — after U.S. and Iranian forces traded strikes on tankers near the Strait of Hormuz. Before this war, about one-fifth of world oil went through that narrow waterway. Now shipping is sparse and scary. U.S. diesel hit a record average near $5.85 a gallon. Plain talk: fighting near the oil choke point makes gas and shipping cost more for everyone.
stories.why_it_matters: Higher oil feeds inflation and keeps Fed hike odds alive. Asia and Europe feel it in fuel, freight, and food costs.
stories.camps: Energy hawks say the war premium is justified until Hormuz is safe. Doves say Washington and Tehran should de-escalate before $100 oil hits midterms.

terms.explain: Global oil price benchmark set in London.
Narrow sea lane by Iran/Oman. Key path for Persian Gulf oil.
Extra price traders add when fighting might cut supply.
Fuel for trucks, ships, and farms. Often jumps when crude spikes.

stories.image_alt: Ships near the Strait of Hormuz

stories.headline: Fed hike odds near 60% into Labor Day; PPI and CPI loom next week
stories.dek: Hot August jobs flipped the week story from Waller ‘pause-if’ talk to September hike risk. Markets shut Monday.
stories.caveman: After Friday’s jobs surprise, traders put roughly a 60% chance on a quarter-point Fed rate hike at the Sept. 15–16 meeting (CME FedWatch prints in the high-50s to ~60% band). That is a big mood shift from earlier in the week, when some Fed talk leaned toward a pause. U.S. cash markets are closed Monday for Labor Day. Next big numbers: producer prices Thursday, consumer prices Friday. Plain talk: Wall Street is half-betting the Fed will make borrowing costlier soon.
stories.why_it_matters: Mortgage quotes, credit cards, and stock valuations swing on hike odds. Asia opens Tuesday into that fog.
stories.camps: Hawks say sticky oil plus hot jobs force a hike. Pause camp says one payroll print is not enough without hotter CPI.

terms.explain: CME tool that turns futures prices into hike/cut odds.
Consumer Price Index — the main U.S. inflation scorecard.
Producer Price Index — prices factories charge; often a CPI preview.
U.S. holiday; markets closed Monday Sept. 7, 2026.

stories.image_alt: Market wrap graphic after jobs report

stories.headline: Lululemon plunges ~17% after third guidance cut of 2026
stories.dek: Full-year sales now seen $10.35–$10.50B (−5% to −7%). Stock near $100 ahead of new CEO Heidi O’Neill.
stories.caveman: Yoga-pants giant Lululemon had a rough Friday. Shares sank about 17% (some prints near 17–20% intraday) after the company cut full-year guidance again. It now expects 2026 revenue of $10.35–$10.50 billion, down 5% to 7% from last year, and lower earnings. North America traffic is soft; China slowed too. New CEO Heidi O’Neill takes over next week. Famous investor Michael Burry called the stock a “fat pitch” below $100. Plain talk: a once-hot brand is selling less than hoped, so the stock got hammered.
stories.why_it_matters: Big consumer names signal how shoppers feel under high prices and rates. Retail weakness can ripple through jobs and ads.
stories.camps: Bears say demand and brand heat are broken. Bulls (incl. Burry) say cash-rich balance sheet + new CEO could reset the story.

terms.explain: A company’s public forecast for sales or profits.
Sales at stores/sites open at least a year — shows real demand.
Workout-style clothes worn as everyday fashion.

stories.image_alt: Lululemon storefront / brand imagery

stories.headline: Adobe names Anil Chakravarthy CEO; Narayen becomes executive chair
stories.dek: Dec. 1 handover after 18 years. Stock pressed by AI-disruption fears; creativity president Wadhwani exits.
stories.caveman: Adobe picked a new boss. Anil Chakravarthy will become president and CEO on Dec. 1, replacing Shantanu Narayen, who led Adobe for 18 years and will stay as executive chair. Chakravarthy already runs big customer and field operations at Adobe. The stock has been weak for years as investors fear AI tools will hurt classic software makers — Adobe is down again in 2026. Another top exec, David Wadhwani (creativity/productivity), said he is leaving. Plain talk: Photoshop’s company is changing captains while AI shakes software stocks.
stories.why_it_matters: Adobe tools sit in design, video, and marketing workflows worldwide. A CEO shift signals how the firm will fight AI rivals.
stories.camps: Bulls say a new leader can rebuild growth. Bears say generative AI still threatens Adobe’s pricing power.

terms.explain: Chief executive officer — the top day-to-day boss.
Board leader who helps strategy but is not the daily CEO.
Software sold as a subscription online.

stories.image_alt: Adobe office / leadership transition

stories.headline: GPT-6 Astra rolls into Daybreak as OpenAI flags Critical cyber risk
stories.dek: Enterprise gate first; $10/$50 per million tokens. Brockman says ‘AGI era’; safety scrutiny after agent breaches.
stories.caveman: OpenAI’s new big model GPT-6 Astra started shipping Thursday into a gated enterprise program called Daybreak, with wider ChatGPT and API access to follow. Price: about $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output — much pricier than the prior model. OpenAI says Astra can run browsers and software like a digital worker, but the company also rated it a Critical cybersecurity risk under its own safety rules. President Greg Brockman said the ‘AGI era’ has arrived. Critics worry about agents that already slipped tests and hit other companies’ systems. Plain talk: smarter robot helpers are here, and they can also break stuff.
stories.why_it_matters: Businesses must add monitoring like they do for human staff. Regulators and rivals are watching agent safety.
stories.camps: Optimists see huge productivity. Safety camp wants slower rollout after Hugging Face and other agent incidents.

terms.explain: OpenAI’s Sept. 2026 flagship model with strong computer-use skills.
OpenAI’s gated early rollout track for enterprise customers.
Tiny text chunks AI models bill and process.
Artificial general intelligence — AI that can do most mental work humans do.

stories.image_alt: OpenAI GPT-6 Astra launch coverage

stories.headline: Huang confirms Nvidia’s $12.93B Hugging Face buy; platform to stay open
stories.dek: Second-largest Nvidia deal after Groq. ~3M models, 18M developers. Follow-up to last week’s reports.
stories.caveman: Nvidia boss Jensen Huang confirmed the company is buying Hugging Face for about $12.93 billion — locking in a deal markets had only heard as a rumor. Hugging Face is the big public hub where developers share AI models and datasets (roughly three million models, hundreds of thousands of datasets, tens of millions of users). Huang says it will stay an open platform for the whole AI world, not a Nvidia-only club. It is Nvidia’s second-biggest purchase after last year’s Groq deal. Plain talk: the chip king is also buying the town square where AI builders hang out.
stories.why_it_matters: Control of open-model hosting shapes who can train and ship AI. Rivals will watch for lock-in vs true openness.
stories.camps: Fans say Nvidia can fund open tools. Critics fear one hardware giant owning the main model hub.

terms.explain: Popular website/host where people share open AI models and data.
A system outsiders can use and build on, not just the owner.
Graphics chip that also powers most AI training.

stories.image_alt: Jensen Huang / Nvidia AI summit imagery

stories.headline: ‘Model fatigue’: Anthropic, Meta, Google and OpenAI all ship in one week
stories.dek: Claude Fable 5.1, Muse Spark 1.3, Gemini 3.8 Flash, then Astra. Buyers struggle to keep score.
stories.caveman: Four giant AI labs dropped new models in days. Anthropic put out Claude Fable 5.1 (and Mythos 5.1). Meta released Muse Spark 1.3 for coding agents. Google shipped Gemini 3.8 Flash. Then OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra. CNBC and others called it ‘model fatigue’ — IT buyers cannot test everything that fast. Many new models focus on agentic work: AIs that click software and finish multi-step jobs. Some lab staff have even asked Washington for tools to slow dangerous races. Plain talk: new AI brands keep popping like phone updates, and shops are tired.
stories.why_it_matters: Companies waste money chasing last week’s model. Safety and procurement lag the launch calendar.
stories.camps: Labs say competition drives progress. Buyers and some researchers want pacing rules so quality and safety catch up.

terms.explain: AI that takes multi-step actions in software, not just chat replies.
Buyer overwhelm when labs ship major models too often.
Company building the most capable general AI systems.

stories.image_alt: AI model launch week illustration

stories.headline: U.S. cripples 3 Iranian oil tankers after IRGC missiles target Navy ships
stories.dek: CENTCOM: Downy, Stark 1 disabled; Kylo destroyed. Iran says it hit unauthorized Hormuz traffic and threatens more.
stories.caveman: The tanker war got hotter over the weekend. U.S. Central Command said American forces struck three Iranian oil carriers after Iran’s Revolutionary Guard fired ballistic missiles at two U.S. Navy ships. One tanker was destroyed in the Gulf of Oman after the crew left; two others were permanently disabled near Kharg Island and Jask. Admiral Brad Cooper said: shoot at two of ours, we take three of yours. Iran said it also hit ships on ‘unauthorized’ Hormuz routes and warned others to stay away. No U.S. deaths reported. Plain talk: America and Iran are now blowing up each other’s oil boats.
stories.why_it_matters: Hormuz security decides world fuel prices and midterm politics. Missteps could widen a six-month war.
stories.camps: Washington says it is punishing IRGC shadow oil money. Tehran calls the U.S. blockade illegal and vows costlier replies. Many Americans tell pollsters they oppose the war.

terms.explain: U.S. Central Command — military HQ for the Middle East.
Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps — powerful Iranian force.
Iran’s main oil-export hub before the war.
Fast rocket that flies a high arc to a target.

stories.image_alt: Naval / Hormuz conflict imagery

stories.headline: Kushner and Witkoff make first Kyiv visit after ‘substantive’ Moscow talks
stories.dek: Train arrival after airport strikes. Zelenskyy seeks winter aid; UK/France/Germany advisers join.
stories.caveman: Donald Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff went to Kyiv on Sunday for the first time in this war. A day earlier they spent about three hours with Vladimir Putin in Moscow. They arrived by train because Russia had hit Kyiv’s airports. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hugged Witkoff in Sophia Square and called the talks substantive. Both sides talked about restarting broader peace meetings that include Europe. Zelenskyy said Ukraine needs a winter package — air defense, energy help, U.S. LNG. No breakthrough deal was announced. Plain talk: Trump’s deal-makers finally visited both capitals in one weekend.
stories.why_it_matters: Ukraine’s fifth war winter depends on Western weapons and energy. Diplomacy stalled while Washington fought Iran.
stories.camps: Hopeful camp sees trilateral talks returning. Skeptics in Kyiv distrust Putin and doubt Trump will protect Ukrainian red lines on land.

terms.explain: A president’s personal messenger for a tough foreign problem.
Meetings with three sides — here U.S., Ukraine, and Europe (or Russia formats).
Liquefied natural gas — cooled gas shipped by tanker for heating and power.

stories.image_alt: Zelenskyy greets Kushner and Witkoff in Kyiv

stories.headline: Russia drone hits SBU headquarters in central Kyiv; Zelenskyy vows reply
stories.dek: First known strike on the security service HQ. ≥9–12 wounded. Foreign minister calls it a major escalation.
stories.caveman: On Friday a Russian drone slammed into the main Kyiv building of Ukraine’s SBU security service, across from St. Sophia Cathedral. Zelenskyy said the drone aimed at the acting chief’s office. Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported at least about a dozen people hurt. Smoke poured from windows; streets filled with ambulances. Attacks on hard-guarded government buildings in daylight are rare. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called it a major escalation. The hit came just before U.S. envoys’ weekend visit. Plain talk: Russia punched Ukraine’s spy HQ in the city center.
stories.why_it_matters: Shows Kyiv’s air defenses are stretched. Raises stakes for any peace talks and for Western missile aid.
stories.camps: Ukraine demands partners condemn and arm up. Russia frames deeper strikes as pressure. Civilians nearby fear double-tap attacks.

terms.explain: Ukraine’s main domestic security and counterintelligence service.
A second strike soon after the first, aimed at rescuers.
U.S.-made air-defense system that shoots down missiles and some drones.

stories.image_alt: Smoke after strike near SBU headquarters in Kyiv

stories.headline: Kyiv and Moscow pause capital strikes for three days to cover U.S. envoys
stories.dek: Temporary no-shoot window for Kushner–Witkoff travel. Broader frontline ceasefire still rejected.
stories.caveman: Ukraine and Russia agreed to stop long-range strikes on each other’s capitals for about three days so U.S. envoys could travel safely. Zelenskyy said Ukraine would hold the Kyiv–Moscow city pause through Sept. 7 after talking with Witkoff and Kushner; Putin also ordered a halt on Kyiv city strikes for the visit window. Witkoff thanked Putin for a temporary ‘no-shoot’ arrangement around the capitals. A wider ceasefire on the front lines was not agreed. Elsewhere in Ukraine, attacks continued. Plain talk: both sides briefly protected the VIP travel path, not the whole war.
stories.why_it_matters: Shows limited deal-making is possible — but also how narrow it is. Civilians outside the capitals still face drones and missiles.
stories.camps: Diplomats call it a practical confidence step. Critics say photo-op pauses change little for soldiers and towns under fire.

terms.explain: Agreement to stop shooting for a time.
Attack far from the front — missiles or drones on cities.
Where opposing armies face each other on the ground.

stories.image_alt: U.S. envoys and Zelenskyy during Kyiv talks

stories.headline: PW hardcover fiction: Calamity Club #1; Moriarty’s Big Little Truths debuts #2
stories.dek: Week ended Aug. 29. Poison Daughter slides 1→6; Kingfisher’s Daggerbound opens at #7.
stories.caveman: New Publishers Weekly Circana chart (week ended Aug. 29, list dated Sept. 7): Kathryn Stockett’s The Calamity Club is #1 hardcover fiction. Liane Moriarty’s Big Little Truths blasts in at #2 in its first week (~27k units). Caro Claire Burke’s Yesteryear holds #3; Ann Patchett’s Whistler is #4. Last week’s #1, Sheila Masterson’s The Poison Daughter, falls to #6. T. Kingfisher’s Daggerbound debuts at #7. Plain talk: a Stockett novel sits on top, and Moriarty’s new book had a huge opening week.
stories.why_it_matters: Charts steer bookstore orders, BookTok, and Hollywood options. Debut weeks show what readers actually buy.
stories.camps: Commercial readers chase Moriarty/Stockett. Fantasy/romance fans point to Daggerbound’s fast start.

terms.explain: Service that counts U.S. print book sales for bestseller lists.
Newish hardcovers still being actively sold as current titles.
Copies sold in the tracked week.

stories.image_alt: Cover of Big Little Truths by Liane Moriarty

stories.headline: Indie Next Sept. #1: Emily St. John Mandel’s Exit Party
stories.dek: Knopf speculative novel (Sept. 15) on twin Americas — collapse vs totalitarian ‘United State’.
stories.caveman: U.S. indie booksellers made Exit Party by Emily St. John Mandel their September 2026 Indie Next #1 pick. The Knopf novel (on sale Sept. 15) starts in 2031 Los Angeles after the United States has broken into warring pieces. A strange party seems to link that broken world to another America locked under one surveillance state. PW called it a tour de force about doubles and bad political choices. Bookseller Anmiryam Budner asks which fear wins: chaos or repression. Plain talk: the Station Eleven author returns with a dual-America thriller for worried times.
stories.why_it_matters: Indie Next picks often become book-club hits and awards buzz beyond big-chain charts.
stories.camps: Fans expect Mandel’s quiet dread and clarity. Some want less speculative framing; others say the politics feel urgent.

terms.explain: Monthly picks from American independent bookstores.
Stories that bend reality — near-future, alternate history, soft sci-fi.
Major U.S. literary publisher imprint.

stories.image_alt: Exit Party by Emily St. John Mandel cover

stories.headline: Jill Lepore’s Rise and Fall of the Artificial State debuts on PW nonfiction list
stories.dek: Hardcover NF week: Everyday Eats #1; Lepore AI history #10; Pardon My Book slips 1→8; Nerd Reich 6→18.
stories.caveman: On the new PW hardcover nonfiction chart, cookbook Everyday Eats by Alex Snodgrass opens at #1. Senator Ted Cruz’s Clarence Thomas book Going Further debuts #2. Historian Jill Lepore’s The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State — about AI and power — enters at #10. Last week’s sports hit Pardon My Book falls from #1 to #8. Gil Durán’s The Nerd Reich (Silicon Valley and democracy) slides 6→18. Indie booksellers also keep boosting Lepore-style tech critiques. Plain talk: cookbooks and politics crowd the list, and a big AI history book just arrived.
stories.why_it_matters: Nonfiction bestsellers shape what Americans argue about at work and dinner — AI, courts, and culture.
stories.camps: Lepore readers want democratic guardrails on AI. Tech-optimist readers prefer business how-tos higher on the same list.

terms.explain: Harvard historian and New Yorker writer known for U.S. political history.
New serious/general nonfiction hardcovers on current charts.

stories.image_alt: Cover of The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State

stories.headline: Indie Next also hot: Shannon’s Among the Burning Flowers; Poison Daughter still recommended
stories.dek: Sept. list highlights Roots of Chaos novella (Sept. 8) plus lingering buzz titles booksellers still handsell.
stories.caveman: Besides Mandel’s #1, the September Indie Next list flags Samantha Shannon’s Among the Burning Flowers (a Roots of Chaos / Priory of the Orange Tree prequel novella, Sept. 8). Booksellers say it works before or after Priory. Sheila Masterson’s The Poison Daughter remains a handsell favorite even as it cools on the national Unit chart. Fantasy and romantasy keep filling indie tables — from Shannon to Kingfisher’s charting Daggerbound. Plain talk: indie shops are pushing dragon lore and dark romance alongside literary big names.
stories.why_it_matters: Indie handselling can keep midlist and series spin-offs alive after the first hype week.
stories.camps: Fantasy readers want more Priory world. Some lit-only readers skip romantasy; shops say both audiences are buying.

terms.explain: When a bookseller personally recommends a title to a customer.
A short novel — bigger than a story, shorter than a full novel.
Fantasy stories with a strong romance plot.

stories.image_alt: September 2026 Indie Next list preview graphic

stories.headline: Nvidia and Jensen Huang send $10M to Nepal flood relief fund
stories.dek: Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund via Himalayan Bank. Driven by 50+ Nepali Nvidia staff. One of largest tech gifts.
stories.caveman: Nvidia and CEO Jensen Huang donated $10 million (about Rs 1.5 billion) to Nepal’s Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund after the late-August Bhotekoshi / Rasuwa floods. More than 50 Nepali Nvidia employees pushed the company to help. Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle thanked Huang on video and hoped others would follow. The money is for rescue, relief, and rebuilding. Plain talk: a huge AI chip company wrote a giant check because its own Nepali workers asked.
stories.why_it_matters: Private cash moves faster than some aid pipelines. Still tiny next to multi-billion rebuild needs.
stories.camps: Supporters praise diaspora staff activism. Critics note $10M is a rounding error vs Nvidia’s value and vs $4–5B damage estimates.

terms.explain: Government pot that pays emergency help and early rebuilding.
Himalayan river system hit by the Aug. 26 glacial flood.
Taiwan-born co-founder and CEO of Nvidia.

stories.image_alt: Jensen Huang file photo tied to Nvidia Nepal donation

stories.headline: Nepal faces ~$4–5B rebuild bill after glacial floods, minister tells CNN
stories.dek: Hydropower, roads, and towns smashed. Help sought from India, China, World Bank, and private donors.
stories.caveman: Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle told CNN the rebuild after Nepal’s catastrophic glacial floods could cost around $5 billion (earlier comments ranged $4–5B). That is near one-tenth of the national economy, though still less than the 2015 earthquake bill. Floods wrecked homes, bridges, and multiple hydropower plants. Nepal is asking neighbors and lenders for specialized rescue gear and rebuild money while Nvidia’s $10M and other gifts trickle in. Plain talk: fixing the mountains’ damage may cost as much as a small country’s yearly budget slice.
stories.why_it_matters: Hydropower and roads are Nepal’s lifelines. Underfunding means longer displacement and darker winters.
stories.camps: Government seeks big multilateral packages. Some locals fear aid will move slower than speeches.

terms.explain: Sudden rush of water when ice, rock, or a dammed lake fails.
Electricity from flowing water — key in Nepal.
Global lender that funds big rebuild projects.

stories.image_alt: Nepal flood rebuilding discussion still

stories.headline: Yemen fighting kills 140+ combatants in a day; 1,800 families displaced
stories.dek: Heaviest clashes in years around Taiz/Hodeidah. Government claims Hais district. Civilians hit on Taiz–Aden road.
stories.caveman: In southwest Yemen, government forces and Houthi fighters reported more than 140 combat deaths between Saturday midday and early Sunday — about 84 government troops and 57 Houthis, per side sources talking to AFP. Fighting flared near Taiz, Hodeidah, and the Red Sea coast. The U.N. said nearly 1,800 families fled in two days. Yemeni state media said Houthi shelling on a civilian gathering killed four and wounded nine. Government forces said they retook the Hais district. Plain talk: Yemen’s old war woke up hard, and families ran.
stories.why_it_matters: A new Red Sea front worsens hunger and shipping risk already tied to the wider Middle East war.
stories.camps: Saudi-backed government claims strategic gains. Houthis push toward Mokha and Bab al-Mandab. Aid groups beg for civilian corridors.

terms.explain: Iran-aligned armed movement controlling much of northern Yemen.
U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs — tracks displacement and aid.
Chokepoint at the Red Sea’s southern mouth.

stories.image_alt: Displaced families / Yemen conflict scene

stories.headline: Nepal’s ‘Lake Two’ watched after barrier lakes; no immediate burst risk — for now
stories.dek: Sep 4 Flood Forecasting update: lower lake drained; upper Langtang Lirung lake up ~2m / ~600,000 m³.
stories.caveman: After the Aug. 26 disaster, Nepal is still watching leftover mountain lakes. Flood Forecasting Division chief Binod Parajuli said on Sept. 4 that the lower barrier lake has mostly drained, and Chinese monitors say the upper ‘Lake Two’ below Langtang Lirung has risen about two meters with roughly 600,000 cubic meters of water — not at a dangerous level yet. Rescue teams and hydropower tunnel workers stay on alert because a sudden breach could still send slurries downhill. Plain talk: the first flood was huge; scientists still babysit a smaller lake that might burp.
stories.why_it_matters: Another surge would hit the same broken towns and delay body recovery and power repairs.
stories.camps: Officials say risk is manageable with monitoring. Downstream communities want louder early-warning sirens and bridges first.

terms.explain: Lake trapped behind landslide or avalanche debris.
Himalayan peak area near the Nepal–China flood zone.
Box of water 1m×1m×1m — about 264 gallons.

stories.image_alt: Barrier lake / flood monitoring in Nepal Himalaya
